title: Measurement of pH
locator: Sections 4.1 and 5.1–5.2, pages 12–18. Figure 6.4–3 outlines the measurement.
summary: Calibrate the electrode with traceable buffers on either side of the expected sample pH and check the electrode response. The field procedure covers temperature, stabilization and recording pH in surface water and groundwater.
scope: Aqueous environmental samples measured with a pH electrode. Section 5.2 gives separate guidance for low-conductance waters. The laboratory still needs the manufacturer's buffer and calibration settings for its meter.
rights: Original catalog summary with a link to the USGS field manual.

title: Specific Conductance
locator: Sections 3.1–3.3, meter calibration. Section 4.3, measurements at low or high pH. Section 6, reporting.
summary: USGS describes setting or checking a conductivity cell constant with standards and reporting specific conductance in µS/cm referenced to 25 °C. Section 4.3 gives a way to check whether the meter's temperature correction works for an acidic sample.
scope: Most natural waters measured in the field or laboratory. Below pH 4, standard temperature compensation can give errors up to 50%. Conductivity reflects all mobile ions and does not identify any one dissolved substance.
rights: Original catalog summary with a link to the USGS field manual.

title: Residue, Non-Filterable (Gravimetric, Dried at 103–105 °C)
version: Method 160.2, issued 1971, as printed in Methods for Chemical Analysis of Water and Wastes
summary: A preweighed glass-fiber filter captures suspended residue from a measured volume of water. After washing and drying to constant mass at 103–105 °C, the increase in filter mass gives the suspended solids concentration in mg/L.
scope: Drinking, surface and saline waters and wastewater. Saline samples can leave dissolved salts on the filter. The washing step and the filter's retention characteristics affect what is counted as suspended solids.
rights: Original catalog summary with a link to EPA's published methods collection.

title: Gravimetric Calibration of Volumetric Standards Using an Electronic Balance
publisher: National Institute of Standards and Technology
locator: Sections 2.1–2.4, scope, principle, equipment and preparation. Section 2.5 and following, procedures by vessel type.
summary: An electronic balance measures the mass of water a vessel contains or delivers. Water temperature determines density for converting mass to volume. The SOP accounts for air buoyancy, the balance calibration and the way the operator sets the meniscus.
scope: Applies when the combined vessel and water load fits the balance and its resolution meets the uncertainty target. Micropipettes require additional evaporation corrections.
rights: Original catalog summary with a link to the NIST procedure.

title: An Interlaboratory Test of pH Measurements in Rainwater
publisher: Journal of Research of the National Bureau of Standards
locator: Table 1, composition of the test solutions. Tables 4 and 5 and accompanying discussion, normalization and laboratory variance.
summary: Koch and colleagues compared laboratories measuring dilute acidic solutions. Referencing results to a dilute acid working standard brought the between-laboratory standard deviation down from about 0.07 to 0.03 pH units.
scope: Evidence of electrode junction effects in low-ionic-strength, rainwater-like samples. The reported improvement in precision applies to the standards and sample types studied.
rights: Original catalog summary with a link to the research paper archived by NIST.

title: A new method of calculating electrical conductivity with applications to natural waters
locator: Authors' abstract, validation in 1,593 water samples and ranges of applicability.
summary: McCleskey and colleagues predicted conductivity from the measured ions and their chemical forms. Comparison with observed conductivity in 1,593 natural water samples gave a reported mean difference of −0.7 ± 5%.
scope: Useful for cross-checking measured conductivity against a chemical analysis. The study covers 30–70,000 µS/cm and requires information about dissolved ions and temperature to calculate the prediction.
rights: Original catalog summary based on the authors' abstract published by USGS.

title: Comparability of Suspended-Sediment Concentration and Total Suspended Solids Data
locator: Abstract and Figure 5, difference between paired measurements as a function of sand fraction.
summary: Gray and colleagues compared 3,235 paired measurements of suspended-sediment concentration and total suspended solids. As the proportion of sand increased, the whole-sample sediment measurement commonly exceeded the result from a solids subsample.
scope: Natural surface-water samples with suspended sediment. This is evidence for considering particle-size distribution and how a subsample is taken before comparing results from the two procedures.
rights: Original catalog summary with a link to the USGS primary study.
